client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately because my final exams are coming up next month, and I'm honestly terrified about my statistics class especially. I've been struggling in that class all semester and I just don't see how things are going to turn out okay. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because at the end of the day I still have to actually pass the exam, you know?
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of fear and pressure right now, and that worry about statistics on top of everything else makes complete sense given how the semester has gone. You're also raising something really honest — that talking alone won't write the exam for you, and I respect that realism. I'm curious though: when you imagine things *not* turning out okay, what does that specific outcome look like in your mind?

client: Honestly, when I picture it going badly, I see myself failing the exam and then failing the whole course, and then maybe losing my financial aid because my GPA drops too low. And then it just spirals in my head — like, what does that mean for my future, my degree, everything I've been working toward? It's like one bad grade becomes this catastrophic ending to everything, and I know that sounds dramatic but it genuinely feels that way when I'm lying awake at night thinking about it.
therapist: It doesn't sound dramatic at all — that spiral you're describing, where one exam becomes the end of everything you've worked for, is genuinely exhausting to carry around, especially in those quiet moments at night. What you're describing is something we call "catastrophizing" in CBT — your mind is jumping from a possible difficulty all the way to the worst imaginable outcome, skipping over all the steps and possibilities in between. I'd love to gently explore that with you — if we look at the actual chain of events, what would *realistically* need to happen for a poor statistics grade to truly derail your entire future?

client: I mean, okay, when I actually think it through — I'd have to fail the class entirely, and then my GPA would have to drop below a certain threshold, and then financial aid would have to actually pull my funding, which I guess isn't automatic. But here's the thing, even knowing that logically doesn't really make the fear go away at night, it still feels just as real and urgent. So I'm not sure how just mapping out the steps is supposed to change how terrified I feel in the moment.
therapist: You've just done something really important — you separated what you *know* from what you *feel*, and that gap is actually at the heart of why this is hard, not a sign that CBT isn't working for you. Logic doesn't automatically overwrite fear, especially when it's been rehearsed so many times at night that your brain has started treating the catastrophe as almost certain. What do you think it would take — even a small shift — to make those nighttime moments feel even slightly less terrifying?

client: I guess maybe if I actually had some kind of plan for the studying, like concrete steps I was taking, it might make the spiral feel a little less out of control at night. But honestly, even when I've tried to make study plans before, I end up either not sticking to them or just feeling guilty when I fall behind, which almost makes things worse. So I'm a little skeptical that a plan alone is going to fix the fear, because I've tried that and it hasn't really worked for me before.
therapist: You're being really thoughtful here — you're not just looking for a quick fix, you're noticing a pattern where plans have actually added *guilt* to the fear rather than relieving it, which is such an important thing to recognize. It sounds like the problem might not be the plan itself, but the story you tell yourself when you inevitably don't follow it perfectly — that falling behind means something bigger about you or your chances. What tends to go through your mind in those moments when you realize you've fallen behind on a plan you made?

client: When I fall behind, my first thought is usually something like "see, I knew you couldn't do this" — like it confirms some deeper fear that I'm just not cut out for this level of work. And then I feel this wave of guilt, like I've wasted time I didn't have, and it becomes really hard to even sit down and start again because what's the point if I'm already behind. It's almost like falling behind once gives me permission to just give up entirely, which I know doesn't make sense but that's where my head goes.
therapist: That voice that says "see, I knew you couldn't do this" is really worth paying attention to — it's not just a reaction to falling behind, it sounds like it's been waiting for evidence to confirm something you already fear about yourself, and that's an incredibly heavy thing to carry into studying. What's also striking is how that one moment of falling behind becomes "permission to quit," as if anything less than perfect execution means the whole effort is worthless — which is actually a really common but painful thinking pattern called all-or-nothing thinking. I'm wondering — if a close friend told you they'd fallen a day behind on their study plan, would you tell them "see, you were never cut out for this"?

client: No, obviously I wouldn't say that to a friend — I'd probably tell them one day doesn't matter that much and to just pick back up where they left off. But it feels different when it's me, like I don't extend myself the same kind of patience I would give someone else. I get what you're pointing at with that comparison, but honestly knowing I'd be kinder to a friend doesn't automatically make me kinder to myself — it kind of just makes me feel worse that I can't seem to do that.
therapist: That self-awareness you just showed is actually really significant — you can see the double standard clearly, and the fact that it makes you feel *worse* rather than better tells me this isn't about lacking insight, it's about something deeper that makes you feel like you don't quite deserve that same kindness. That gap between knowing and feeling is real, and it's not a personal failing — it often points to beliefs we've held about ourselves for a long time that take more than one conversation to soften. I'm curious — where do you think that harsher inner standard came from, has it always been there or can you trace it back to something?

client: I think it's been there for a long time, honestly — I grew up in a house where doing well academically was kind of the main way I felt like I mattered, so anything less than excellent always felt like a personal failure rather than just a normal mistake. I can trace it back to that pretty clearly, but I'm not sure what I'm supposed to do with that information — like, knowing where it came from doesn't automatically make it stop. It almost feels like opening a door I'm not sure I'm ready to walk through right now, especially with exams a month away.
therapist: You've just made a really meaningful connection, and it takes courage to see that clearly — that your worth got tangled up with your performance at a young age, and that's not a small thing. And I want to honor what you just said about the timing, because you're right that this isn't the moment to fully unpack all of that, and it's actually wise self-awareness to recognize that boundary rather than forcing it. So given that we want to keep one eye on getting you through these exams, what would it look like to just *borrow* that kinder friend-voice for the next month, not as a permanent fix, but just as a temporary tool to help you keep moving forward?

client: I like the idea of framing it as "borrowing" rather than like, completely rewiring how I think about myself, that actually feels a little less overwhelming. But I'm not sure how to do that in practice when I'm in the middle of a panic spiral at midnight — like, the kinder voice feels really far away in those moments and the harsh one is just so much louder. I guess I'm asking, is there something more concrete I can do in that actual moment, because just telling myself "be kinder" doesn't feel like enough when the anxiety is already at full volume?
therapist: You're asking exactly the right question, and the fact that you're thinking ahead to that midnight moment shows real self-awareness — the harsh voice *is* louder when anxiety is already running high, so "just be kinder" is genuinely not enough on its own. One concrete thing that can help is having a specific, pre-written phrase ready — something like "I'm behind, and that's uncomfortable, but behind isn't over" — that you've chosen *before* the spiral, so you're not trying to generate compassion from scratch when you have nothing left. Would it feel useful to try crafting something like that together right now, something that feels true enough that even your skeptical, anxious midnight-self might be able to hold onto it?

client: I'm actually a little open to trying that, which surprises me because I usually roll my eyes at stuff like affirmations or mantras. But my worry is that in the moment, it'll just feel hollow or like I'm lying to myself, especially if I'm already convinced things are falling apart. Can we make it something that doesn't sound too positive or forced, because I think I'd actually reject it if it felt like I was trying to trick myself into feeling okay?
therapist: I love that you're open to this *and* holding onto your skepticism at the same time — that's actually the perfect combination, because you're right that something falsely cheerful would just bounce off you in that moment. The key is making it honest rather than positive, something that acknowledges the difficulty without catastrophizing it — so less "everything will be fine!" and more something like "this feels awful right now, and I've survived awful before" or "I'm struggling, and struggling doesn't mean failing." What words feel true to you — not reassuring, just *accurate* — that you think your midnight-self could actually believe?

client: Something like "this is hard and I'm scared, but one bad night doesn't decide anything" feels closer to something I could actually believe. It's not pretending everything is fine, it's just kind of... pumping the brakes on the spiral without lying to myself about how bad it feels. I'm still not a hundred percent sure I'll actually remember to use it in the moment, but it feels less fake than anything I've tried before.
therapist: That phrase you just came up with is really good — it's honest, it's grounded, and it respects your intelligence rather than trying to paper over the fear. The worry about remembering it in the moment is valid, so it might help to make it physical somehow — writing it on a sticky note by your desk or saving it as a note on your phone so it's there *before* you need it, not something you have to conjure from memory at midnight. How are you feeling right now compared to when we started talking — even just a little?
